data.title: FDA expands J&J’s Rybrevant Faspro label with head and neck cancer approval
data.description:
The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has authorised Johnson & Johnson’s (J&J) Rybrevant Faspro (amivantamab and hyaluronidase-lpuj) for certain patients with head and neck cancer, marking the first dual-targeted therapy in this setting.

The accelerated approval is for the treatment of adults with recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) whose disease has progressed on or after platinum–based chemotherapy and an anti–PD–(L)1 antibody. HNSCC is the most common form of head and neck cancer, a group of cancers that arise in the mouth, throat, voice box, sinuses, nasal cavity, and salivary glands.

Rybrevant is a bispecific antibody that targets epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and mesenchymal-epithelial transition (MET), two key drivers of tumour progression. Together, the two genes are overexpressed in up to 90% of recurrent and metastatic HNSCC tumours. Rybrevant is an intravenous product, though Rybrevant Faspro is co-formulated with Halozyme’s recombinant human hyaluronidase, allowing it to be administered via a subcutaneous injection. The drug blocks signals that tell cancer cells to divide and grow.

The FDA based its accelerated approval on results from the Phase Ib/II OrigAMI-4 trial (NCT06385080) that demonstrated an overall response rate (ORR) of 42% in patients taking the drug. The time to achieve response was fast, with the median time to first response arriving at 6.6 weeks. Of the responders, 56% maintained a response for more than six months.

Amanda Hollinger, executive director at the Head and Neck Cancer Alliance, said: “For people living with recurrent or metastatic head and neck cancer, the stakes are incredibly high. I’ve seen firsthand that when the disease progresses, patients often face limited treatment options, while managing symptoms that can affect their ability to eat, speak, swallow and breathe. At a time when treatment advances are urgently needed to improve outcomes for patients, this new option offers renewed hope for patients and their families.”

J&J stated that readouts from the Phase III OrigAMI-5 study in first-line HNSCC could be called upon by the FDA for continued approval.

J&J’s Rybrevant will now compete with MSD’s Keytruda (pembrolizumab) and Bristol Myers Squibb’s Opdivo (nivolumab), both types of immunotherapies, on the US HNSCC market. Approved targeted therapies in this indication include Eli Lilly’s antibody Erbitux (cetuximab). However, unlike Rybrevant, Erbitux only targets EGFR.

Approval in HNSCC marks the first indication beyond lung cancer for Rybrevant Faspro. The therapy is approved for four indications within lung cancer.  

Rybrevant has been highlighted as a primary growth driver for J&J over the next decade. By 2030, J&J is aiming to generate $50bn in annual oncology sales – Rybrevant is expected to contribute to this as it notches more indications.

Analysis by Pharmaceutical Technology’s parent company, GlobalData, forecasts that Rybrevant will generate $2.6bn in global sales in 2030, though the model does not include the addition of an HNSCC indication.

data.title: MHRA champions patient voices through new policy
data.description:
The UK’s Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) has unveiled a policy to enhance the role of patients and the public in forming drug and medical device regulation. 

Dubbed the Patient and Public Involvement and Engagement (PPIE) Plan 2026-2030, the agency designed the policy to facilitate earlier and wider engagement with both communities and patient groups – allowing it to better consider unique patient needs while shaping its regulatory strategy. 

Through this policy, the MHRA plans to inform its decisions through the lived experience of patients. This means that the regulator will consider their opinions when drafting new policies, conducting safety reviews and assessing the risk-benefit profile of a drug or device, as well as how it should govern emerging technologies like artificial intelligence (AI). 

This plan builds on the MHRA’s recently announced Strategy 2030, in which the agency aims to streamline drug and device regulation, while working on making the process more patient-centric. 

Through PPIE, the MHRA also hopes to hear from a more diverse group of patients by expanding its Patient and Public Community, which will guide the agency in making information about medicines more accessible for all. The MHRA first established this patient group in 2024 to unite patients, charities and patient organisations in a bid to guide MHRA decision-making. 

On top of this, the regulator will also work on improving its systems, which it hopes to achieve by strengthening feedback and reporting for greater patient transparency on how their contributions influence decision-making. This will also see the MHRA focus on improving its work with the UK’s health watchdog, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), by diminishing duplication within its patient involvement evidence database.  

Thus far, patient involvement has already benefited the MHRA, the agency says, as an advisory group of 23 patient representatives has helped to inform draft guidance and identify key priorities within the context of rare disease. 

According to the MHRA’s chair, Anthony Harnden, this plan represents “a vital evolution” in the agency’s approach to patient engagement, as the healthcare landscape enters a period of rapid change. 

“Patients and the public can tell us how treatments affect their everyday lives, what benefits they value most and where information needs to be clearer,” Harnden said, adding that the insights will allow the regulator to ask the right questions and make better informed regulatory decisions. 

MHRA targets widespread reform 

The MHRA debuts PPIE as it looks to enact wider reforms to its regulatory approach, with the agency also looking to release a Women’s Health Plan later this year. 

To keep up with the changing landscape, the MHRA is also figuring out the best ways to regulate AI – both when reviewing drug and device applications, and when incorporating it into its own workflow.  

This shift can also be seen within wider government initiatives. Recently, British ministers backed all 44 recommendations around AI-enabled medical devices made by its National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare. 

The UK government reforms its approach as global life sciences and healthcare competition mounts – with key established players like the US and up-and-coming leaders like China increasingly attracting attention on the global stage.

data.title: Armada to combine with Brains Bioceutical in $750m deal
data.description:
Armada Acquisition has entered a definitive business combination agreement with Brains Bioceutical that values the latter at an implied pre-money equity value of about $750m.

Following completion of the merger, the combined entity will be named Brains Therapeutics and intends to list its common shares on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the BAPI ticker symbol.

The transaction remains subject to regulatory clearances, registration statements, and shareholder votes from both entities.

The boards of directors of both organisations have unanimously approved the deal, which is scheduled to conclude during the second quarter of 2027.

Under the agreed terms, current Brains Bioceutical shareholders will roll the entirety of their equity into the new public company.

Brains Bioceutical manufactures active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) and develops pharmaceutical therapies, operating an EU good manufacturing practice (EU-GMP) manufacturing facility through its wholly owned subsidiary, BSPG Laboratories.

The company produces or develops several cannabinoid ingredients, comprising cannabinol (CBN), cannabidiol (CBD), cannabigerol (CBG), delta-8-tetrahydrocannabinol (D8-THC), and D9-THC, alongside medical products and drug intermediates.

It maintains regulatory filings, controlled-substance licences, and clinical research experience across Australia, Brazil, Japan, the UAE, the UK/EU, and the US.

In addition to pharmaceutical supply, the business distributes ingredients across animal health and nutraceutical markets.

Brains Bioceutical CEO and chairman Rick Brar said: “This transaction represents an important milestone in the evolution of Brains Bioceutical. We have spent years developing the manufacturing, regulatory and scientific foundation required to participate in the pharmaceutical market at scale.

“Today, Brains is not simply developing promising compounds. We have an established pharmaceutical-grade manufacturing platform, commercial customer relationships, extensive regulatory experience and a growing pipeline of proprietary and partnered drug programmes.”

The company’s clinical pipeline includes an oral capsule for epilepsy, an early programme targeting sleep disorders, and global rights to an extended-release methazolamide formulation for glaucoma.

Brains Bioceutical also provides clinical material for a National Institutes of Health (NIH)-funded study assessing cannabinoids for opioid use disorder.

data.title: Alfasigma receives EC’s expanded approval for filgotinib to treat axSpA
data.description:
Alfasigma has received expanded approval from the European Commission (EC) for Jyseleca (filgotinib) to treat adult patients living with active axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA).

The additional indication approval covers radiographic and non-radiographic forms of the chronic inflammatory disease in individuals who show an inadequate response to conventional therapy.

Alfasigma has also submitted a marketing authorisation application to the UK’s Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), which is currently reviewing the filing.

The EC approval is supported by findings from the Phase III OLINGUITO programme published in the Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases.

The clinical programme evaluated the efficacy and safety of oral once-daily filgotinib 200mg compared with placebo across two randomised, double-blind trials: Study A, which recruited 258 patients with radiographic axSpA (r-axSpA); and Study B, which involved 237 participants with non-radiographic axSpA (nr-axSpA).

All enrolled patients met Assessment of SpondyloArthritis international Society criteria and had experienced intolerance or an insufficient response to standard care.

Both trials met their primary endpoint at week 16, demonstrating statistically significant ASAS40 response rates over placebo.

In Study A, 39.5% of filgotinib recipients achieved an ASAS40 response versus 20.9% on placebo, representing an 18.6% treatment difference.

In Study B, 34.5% reached the endpoint compared with 17.8% in the control arm, yielding a 16.7% difference.

Alfasigma global chief portfolio and medical strategy officer Richard Azencoth said: “We welcome the EC’s decision to expand filgotinib’s licence and provide a new treatment option for people living with axSpA in Europe.

“AxSpA is a lifelong condition that presents long-term management challenges, and despite the availability of several advanced therapies, currently half of the patients fail to adequately respond to treatment.

“Approval of a new disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug is an important step for those living with axSpA, and we are working with authorities within Europe to translate approval into appropriate access.”

axSpA typically emerges in patients in their 30s, affecting the axial skeleton and causing persistent back pain and spinal stiffness.

An oral JAK1 preferential inhibitor available in 100mg and 200mg tablets, Jyseleca is already authorised for moderate to severe active rheumatoid arthritis and moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis across the EU, Japan, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, and the UK.

In August 2026, Alfasigma agreed to purchase Nordic Group, a move aimed at strengthening its speciality care business and expanding its reach in Europe, Canada, and Japan.

data.title: Cordavis to stay in CVS Health after bifurcation of $117bn empire
data.description:
CVS Health will keep biosimilar subsidiary Cordavis under its umbrella, after the company announced plans to split off its pharmacy chain from its health business.

On 4 November, CVS Health – the largest US healthcare conglomerate and the world’s second largest healthcare company – revealed plans to separate into two, publicly traded entities. The company had a market capitalisation of around $117bn before a selloff in its shares following the announcement wiped nearly $15bn off its market value.   

The first will be a healthcare solutions company, comprising health networks and insurance service providers Aetna, CVS Caremark, CVS Specialty, Oak Street Health and Signify Health. The other will house its sprawling chain of 9,000 retail pharmacies, along with mail pharmacy, MinuteClinic, and the Health100 technology services business.

The former will be called CVS Health on an interim basis, while the latter will be named CVS Pharmacy. The split is expected to complete by the first half of 2028.

The plans for Cordavis were not revealed in the announcement. A CVS spokesperson confirmed to Pharmaceutical Technology that the unit will remain with the CVS Health company moving forward.

CVS Health established Cordavis in August 2023, aiming to capitalise on the pharma industry’s patent cliff, which was just beginning at the time. Through its model, Cordavis works with biosimilar manufacturers in the US, with parent company CVS relying on its extensive pharmacy network to facilitate access.

“Biosimilars represent one of the biggest opportunities for reducing drug costs for employers and consumers,” the company said in a statement when launching the subsidiary.

There has been a lack of public announcements from the subsidiary since its launch, though it currently markets five biosimilars according to its website. Most notable is ordavis Hyrimoz (adalimumab-adaz), a biosimilar to AbbVie’s Humira. In January 2024, CVS Caremark, the pharmacy benefits management subsidiary of CVS Health, dropped Humira from its list of covered drugs, instead offering biosimilars.

The CVS split follows an increase in scrutiny over the company’s dominant position in the US medical landscape. Lawmakers and politicians have argued that the firm’s dual role as both as retail drugstore chain and pharmacy benefits manager (PBM) have driven the costs up for certain prescription medicines. The creation of Cordavis was therefore significant, given a key aim of the subsidiary is to broaden access to cheaper drugs.  

Biosimilars is just one strategic avenue that CVS undertook as its empire spread to nearly all sectors within American healthcare. CVS’ first store opened in 1963, with a string of business expansions via deals and mergers since. The highest profile of these was the $69bn combination with health insurance company Aetna in 2018. While growth expectations have not met investor expectations, other healthcare giants such as UnitedHealth had followed the CVS model of a vertically integrated insurer and pharmacy business.

CVS Health’s CEO David Joyner said in an earnings call: “We are doing [this plan] because we actually have healthy balance sheets with appropriate capital allocation opportunities and momentum in each of the businesses. I feel really good about the timing. I feel really good about the decision, and I feel equally as important about the team that is going allow us to execute against this plan.”

data.title: Big pharma-backed T-Therapeutics snags $133m to bring TCEs to clinic
data.description:
UK-based biotech T-Therapeutics has netted $133m in a Series B financing round to bring its range of first-in-class T-cell receptor (TCR)-targeting T-cell engager (TCE) therapies for cancer and autoimmune diseases to the clinic. 

With cash in the bank from this oversubscribed round, which was co-led by the British Business Bank and Advent Life Sciences, T-Therapeutics will look to generate clinical proof-of-concept data for both its lead TCR-CD3-targeting bispecific oncology and autoimmune drugs. The round had big pharma involvement too. Eli Lilly, as well as the venture arms of Johnson & Johnson and Sanofi, contributed.  

On the oncology side, T-Therapeutics is developing a programme it says offers “broad therapeutic potential” across the realm of solid tumours. Meanwhile, in immunology, the company is using its platform to develop a precise, novel approach to resetting the immune system – specifically by selectively reducing levels of pathogenic cells that drive chronic inflammation. 

While T-Therapeutics was light on the details for both programmes, the company did note that it designed both to address multiple indications where patients currently have limited treatment options – with the company’s CEO, Theodora Harold, touting their “blockbuster” potential. 

At the core of T-Therapeutics’ approach is its OpTiMus platform, which the British biotech says can unlock access to validated and previously undruggable intracellular targets. This platform comes as progress in developing TCEs for solid tumours remains stifled due to the lack of appropriate targets, says Advent Life Sciences general partners, Dominic Schmidt. 

“By unlocking previously undruggable intracellular targets, with the potential for a markedly improved safety profile, T-Therapeutics’ platform brings the promise of this treatment/modality to solid tumours, where the great majority of cancers arise,” Schmidt commented. 

On top of its newfound capital, T-Therapeutics will also bolster its leadership through this financing round, as representatives from both financing co-leads, as well as Johnson & Johnson’s innovation arm JJDC and Samsara BioCapital will take a seat at the biotech’s board as non-executive directors. 

TCEs attract the big bucks 

T-Therapeutics is part of a growing list of biotechs attracting funding and taking part in deals in the TCE space, as the modality piques the interest of investors and big pharma alike. 

In recent months, several pharma giants have bolstered their pipelines with the modality – Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS), GSK, Gilead, UCB, Boehringer Ingelheim and Sanofi have all forged deals in this area. 

Companies are also broadening their focus towards new areas for TCEs – which have traditionally found the greatest success in the blood cancer space. Now, companies are exploring their potential in solid tumours, as well as autoimmune and infectious diseases. 

In a recent report from GlobalData, parent company of Pharmaceutical Technology, a notable portion of biopharma professionals expressed their view that TCEs will be the modality with the greatest impact in the immunology and dermatology spaces in the next one-to-three years – eclipsed only by monoclonal, bi and trispecific antibodies.

data.title: Podcast: An investor’s guide to preparing your clinical data package
data.description:
In recent years, the biotech financing landscape has been in a period of tumult, with ever-growing competition and shifts in the global policy landscape contributing to a challenging fundraising environment.

While various hurdles remain, biotechs must still find a way to attract investor attention to secure capital to fund their drug development efforts and build up their all-crucial data packages.

In this episode of the GlobalData Healthcare Podcast, recorded at the 2026 Outsourcing in Clinical Trials and Clinical Trial Supply Nordics conference, held in Copenhagen, Denmark, Annabel Kartal-Allen, reporter for Pharmaceutical Technology’s sister publication Clinical Trials Arena, chats with Stephan Christgau, founding partner at Eir Ventures.

He discusses what looks for in a biotech when making investment decisions, and what is catching his eye as an investor in a sea of innovation.

Christgau also elaborates on the importance of developing an effective clinical strategy to garner the trust of a prospective investor – diving into what separates a good data package from a great one, and what he looks for in this realm when allocating capital.

If you liked this episode of the GlobalData Healthcare podcast, you can find a range of episodes, which bring you key insights into the world of pharma, biotech, medical devices and clinical trials, at this link.

data.title: Evommune signs $1.1bn licence deal with Hinova for EVO570
data.description:
Evommune has secured exclusive rights outside Greater China to develop, manufacture and commercialise EVO570, an autoimmune therapy, from Hinova Pharmaceuticals in a licence deal worth up to around $1.1bn.

Evommune will pay $30m upfront, consisting of $20m in cash and $10m in pre-funded warrants for common shares.

Hinova is eligible to receive the remainder of the deal value through development, regulatory, and commercial milestone payments, alongside tiered royalties on net sales outside Greater China.

Earlier designated as HC118, EVO570 is an oral molecular glue degrader designed to target the Vav guanine nucleotide exchange factor 1 (VAV1) signalling protein.

The Hinova-discovered therapy has not yet received regulatory approval.

Regulatory filings for an investigational new drug (IND) have been submitted in China and accepted in the US, with a Phase I trial assessing safety, pharmacokinetics, and target engagement scheduled to start imminently.

Preclinical studies demonstrated activity in animal models of several immune conditions and greater potency in human immune cells than competitor degraders.

Evommune chief scientific officer Dr Jeegar Patel said: “VAV1 is a compelling target in immunology today, offering a potential path to JAK-like efficacy without the safety and tolerability challenges of other available therapies.

“With a differentiated scaffold and structure-guided optimisation resulting in sub-nanomolar potency, high selectivity and a profile supporting once-daily oral dosing, EVO570 has the potential to be a best-in-class approach for patients with rheumatoid arthritis and other T- and B-cell-driven autoimmune diseases.

“We look forward to reporting Phase I results and plan to advance it into its first Phase II trial in rheumatoid arthritis in 2027.”

Advising Hinova on the transaction were BFC Group as exclusive financial adviser and Fangda Partners as exclusive legal adviser.

Hinova has one prostate cancer drug approved in China and is developing small molecules, deuterated drugs, and proteolysis targeting chimera (PROTAC) degraders.

Evommune continues to advance therapies for chronic inflammatory diseases.

data.title: PharmatrophiX and Circular partner on neurodegenerative drugs
data.description:
PharmatrophiX and Circular Genomics have entered a strategic collaboration to advance blood-based circular ribonucleic acid (RNA) biomarkers in neurodegenerative drug development programmes.

The partnership will initially apply blood-based circular RNA profiling to PharmatrophiX’s LM11A-31 in Alzheimer’s, with potential expansion across its neurodegeneration pipeline.

LM11A-31 is the company’s first-in-class small molecule that acts on the p75 neurotrophin receptor (p75NTR) to address mechanisms of neurodegeneration and encourage synaptic resilience.

Under the initial workstream, Circular Genomics will deploy its research-use-only CircPath molecular profiling system to examine baseline molecular differences and track biological pathway shifts during treatment.

The partners intend to combine the circRNA findings with cognitive, clinical, imaging, proteomic, and established Alzheimer’s biomarker metrics to analyse pharmacodynamic responses and patient biology for future clinical studies.

PharmatrophiX CEO David Setboun said: “LM11A-31 is designed to protect brain cells and their connections by targeting underlying mechanisms of neurodegeneration. Understanding how the drug affects these processes in patients is central to our development strategy.

“This strategic collaboration with Circular Genomics will allow us to explore how a simple blood test could provide deeper insights into how patients respond to treatment.

“These findings may also help inform future clinical trials of LM11A-31 and potentially support the development of other therapies across our neurodegeneration pipeline.”

The companies also plan to assess broadening their work into additional neurotrophin-receptor programmes by mutual agreement.

Potential therapeutic areas under consideration include Alzheimer’s disease, HIV-associated dementia, and progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP).

Both organisations also intend to seek joint grants and non-dilutive funding to finance translational biomarker research across their pipelines.

Circular Genomics president and CEO Paul Sargeant said: “The next generation of neurodegenerative drug development will require biomarkers that do more than measure disease burden—they must help us understand the biology changing in response to therapy.

“This collaboration gives us the opportunity to apply circRNA biology to a differentiated therapeutic programme and demonstrate how our platform can provide pathway-level insight into pharmacodynamic response and patient heterogeneity.”

data.title: Trump’s healthcare plans under contention after Democrats’ midterm landslide
data.description:
The Democrats have gained significantly more power to contest the Trump administration’s healthcare agenda after the party won the Senate and the House in the US midterm elections. 

This comes as the Democrats notch a group of Senate victories across traditionally Republican stronghold states such as Texas, Kansas and Ohio. The Democrats hold 54 seats in the Senate compared to 44 for the Republicans, while in the House, they hold 228 compared to 139 for the Republicans (correct at 6.22am EST). 

While votes are still being counted across some states, meaning results could change, the Democrats’ victory is well established, with the party having crossed the threshold for a majority in both, with a majority being 50 in the Senate and 218 in the House. 

This result has given the Democrats their first chance to contest the healthcare policy decisions made by US President Donald Trump and his administration since the 2024 elections. 

Reacting to the Democrats’ midterm sweep, Citi analysts noted that, while healthcare oversight risk may increase, the new development is unlikely to significantly change the near-term biopharma policy backdrop – adding that the existing Most Favored Nation (MFN) agreements will likely remain intact. 

However, they did mention that Democratic committee control “likely brings visible hearings and inquiries around drug pricing, industry practices and implementation”. 

Vaccine policies, staffing changes, and pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) are all likely to feature as points of focus.

In a LinkedIn article, Allianz Global Investors CIO of public markets, Michael Krautzberger and senior US economist and VP, Liam Wash, echoed the sentiments of Citi analysts, noting that the outcome of the midterms largely “points to more political friction than policy transformation”. 

However, like Citi, they pointed to the potential of greater congressional oversight and constraints on the Trump administration to make the policy backdrop “more predictable,” while shifting the relative appeal of sectors. 

“We believe Democrats could address affordability concerns through raising the minimum wage, investigating corporate price-setting techniques, and extending healthcare subsidies, but are likely to face Republican opposition,” Krautzberger and Wash commented. 

Prior to the midterms, senior healthcare economist Diederik Stadig also shared his opinions in an article, where he said that a clean sweep from the Democrats could result in a mixed outcome for pharma. 

This, in his eyes, is because the Democrats are likely to slow MFN momentum by “demanding transparency around the deals, as well as challenging their design and cost”, while prioritising expanding Medicare drug price negotiations agreed under the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), Stadig said. 

However, he did note that the likelihood of stronger congressional protection of key US health agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH), as well as the review capacity of the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), could help to support early-stage innovation and the wider American biotech sector. 

“If Democrats truly make drug-price negotiations a priority, then this scenario could lead to a mixed outcome: greater price pressure, but a stronger public research base and a better-funded FDA,” Stadig noted. 

Possible implications for the MAHA initiative  

With this win, the Democrats have undoubtedly secured more power to contest the Trump administration’s decision-making – potentially throwing a spanner in the works as it looks to enact the Make America Healthy Again initiative brought in by US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr (RFK Jr). 

During his time at the helm of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), RFK Jr has consistently pushed for an upheaval to legacy childhood vaccination schedules, while working to legitimise and democratise the use of unapproved wellness peptides and cut funding to certain modalities, such as mRNA-based vaccines. 

Across the wider administration, Trump has also enforced sweeping cuts to Medicaid through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1), which the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimates could leave 11.8 million people without health insurance by 2034. 

In a press statement, CEO of independent financial advisory organisation, the deVere Group, Nigel Green, noted that healthcare looks set to benefit from the Democrats’ increasing congressional power. 

“Democrats are expected to restore enhanced Affordable Care Act (ACA) subsidies and revisit Republican Medicaid changes,” Green commented, adding that hospitals and insurers are likely to be the “clearest winners”.
